text: Downey is a city in southeastern Los Angeles County, California, United States, located 13 miles (21 kilometers) southeast of Downtown Los Angeles and considered part of the Gateway Cities. It is the birthplace of the Apollo space program and Taco Bell and is home to the world's oldest operating McDonald's restaurant, the Speedee McDonald's Store, which opened in 1953 at the southwest corner of Florence Avenue and Lakewood Boulevard. The store was damaged in the 1994 Northridge Earthquake and reopened in 1996 with a museum and gift shop. As of the 2020 census, the city had a total population of 114,355, with a population density of 9,215.5 inhabitants per square mile (3,558.1/km²). The city covers a total area of 12.6 square miles (33 km²), of which 12.4 square miles (32 km²) is land and 0.2 square miles (0.52 km²) is water. The racial makeup was 23.4% White, 3.7% African American, 2.1% Native American, 6.7% Asian, 0.3% Pacific Islander, 40.0% from other races, and 23.9% from two or more races, with 75.1% of the population identifying as Hispanic or Latino of any race. The city is adjacent to South Gate and Bell Gardens to the west and northwest, Pico Rivera to the northeast, Santa Fe Springs and Norwalk to the east, and Paramount and Bellflower to the south. According to the Köppen Climate Classification system, Downey has a semi-arid climate (BSk). Mission San Gabriel Arcángel was initially founded on September 8, 1771, near Tongva settlements on a bluff overlooking the Rio Hondo, near the modern intersection of San Gabriel Blvd and Lincoln Avenue, and was later relocated to its present site in San Gabriel after five years due to flooding. In 1784, Governor Pedro Fages granted former soldier Manuel Nieto (1734–1804) a land concession of 300,000 acres (120,000 hectares) stretching from the Santa Ana River to the Old San Gabriel River (now the Rio Hondo and Los Angeles River) and from the mission highway (approximately Whittier Boulevard) to the ocean, though the acreage was later reduced due to encroachment on Mission San Gabriel lands. The land, known as Rancho Los Nietos, passed to Manuel Nieto’s four children after his death and was partitioned in 1833 by Mexican Governor José Figueroa; the northwestern portion, including the Downey-Norwalk area, was granted as Rancho Santa Gertrudes to Josefa Cota, widow of Antonio Nieto, covering approximately 21,000 acres (8,500 hectares) and containing the old Nietos homestead, a center of social life east of the pueblo of Los Angeles. Dairy was a major industry, with the Central Milk Agency marketing milk for "seven hundred dairymen whose dairy herds range from thirty to two thousand head" valued at over $1,000,000 per month. Some settlers came from Ireland, and the city was founded and named for John Gately Downey, the former and youngest governor of California, born in Ireland, who supported Republican Lincoln during the Civil War and pioneered modern subdivision development between the Rio Hondo and San Gabriel River around 1865. He believed oranges would flourish in Southern California and imported several varieties, leading to oranges becoming one of the state’s biggest cash crops. Two small settlements—College Settlement and Gallatin—were established along the Rio Hondo River, with Gallatin building a school known as the "Little Red Gallatin School House" in the late 1860s, later expanded to a two-story building in 1871 and moved to its present site in 1893. By 1883, College Settlement, Gallatin, and Downey joined, and with Governor Downey’s efforts, the Southern Pacific Railroad was convinced to route through and stop in Downey, making the depot area the new center of activity and forming a larger Downey. Farmers grew grain, corn, castor beans, and fruit, and by 1935 Downey was characterized as an "orange-grove town." Downey was incorporated in 1956 and adopted a charter form of government in 1964. After World War II, suburban homes and factories replaced farms. During World War II, Vultee Aircraft was Downey’s largest employer, producing 15% of all American military aircraft by 1941 and pioneering the use of women in manufacturing and the first powered assembly line for airplanes. After WWII, the plant was idle from 1945 to 1948 before being occupied by North American Aviation, which later became North American Rockwell, then Rockwell International, and eventually Boeing. In 1961, the facility was transferred to NASA and became the birthplace of the Apollo Space Program and the Space Shuttle, producing and testing many of the 20th century’s greatest aviation, missile, and space endeavors. The Rockwell plant closed in 1999, and the site was demolished and replaced by the Columbia Memorial Space Center, Downey Landing shopping center, Promenade at Downey shopping center (formerly Downey Studios), a Kaiser Permanente hospital, and a city recreation fields park. In the 1960s, Downey Records gained notoriety with recordings such as The Chantays' "Pipeline," and later, the local music scene led to the founding of The Blasters and Dark Angel. Rancho Los Amigos National Rehabilitation Center, the main public rehabilitation hospital for Los Angeles County, is located in Downey and is renowned worldwide for its innovations in spinal cord injury and post-polio syndrome care. Downey was featured in the 2008 film Pineapple Express, with many buildings along Florence Avenue appearing in a driving sequence. In 2010, the population was 111,772 with a density of 8,893.3 inhabitants per square mile (3,433.7/km²), and the median household income was $60,939, with 11.8% of the population below the poverty line. In 2023, the median household income was estimated at $87,400 and the per capita income at $37,122, with 7.0% of families and 9.1% of the population below the poverty line. In 2022, the Greater Los Angeles Homeless Count reported 218 homeless individuals in Downey, with approximately 30–40 homeless residents in the area. Crime reports from 2008 show a drop in robberies, aggravated assaults, and petty thefts, but auto thefts reached a 10-year high with 1,231 vehicles reported stolen, along with 252 robberies, 172 aggravated assaults, 24 rapes, 711 burglaries, and 2,038 larceny/thefts. In the late 1980s and early 1990s, gang activity increased, and although it persists in the southern area today, the city formed GOOD (Gangs Out Of Downey) to engage youth aged 10–20 in anti-gang programs, including sports, after-school care, scholarship programs, and counseling, maintaining a partnership with the Downey Police Department. In 2017, Downey was recognized as L.A. County's "Most Business-Friendly City" by the Los Angeles County Economic Development Corporation. The city is in California's 30th senatorial district, represented by Democrat Bob Archuleta, and the 64th Assembly district, represented by Democrat Blanca Pacheco, and in the 42nd congressional district, represented by Democrat Robert Garcia. Author Tom Wolfe wrote about Downey in his 1968 book "The Pump House Gang," including an article titled "The Hair Boys" about Harvey's Drive-in and the fashion of the hair boys, with a drawing of one appearing in "In Our Time." In 1955, a global news story emerged when truck driver George Di Peso at 7739 Alderdale Street tried to drown a gopher by placing a hose into its hole, only to find the hose being slowly pulled down, which was reported worldwide in a July 3, 1955, Los Angeles Times article titled "Tokyo Awaits Arrival of Downey Hose."

Downey is located in California's 42nd congressional district and is represented by Democrat Robert Garcia. Author Tom Wolfe wrote about Downey in his article "The Hair Boys," which described Harvey's Drive-in and the distinctive fashions worn by the hair boys, claiming Harvey's was one of the world's great unacknowledged centers of fashion. The essay appears in Wolfe's 1968 book "The Pump House Gang," and a drawing of a hair boy is included in his book "In Our Time." In 1955, Downey gained international attention when truck driver George Di Peso, living at 7739 Alderdale Street, attempted to eliminate a gopher by placing a hose into its hole and turning on the water, only to find the hose disappearing into the ground. Wire services reported the incident worldwide, and a July 3, 1955, front-page Los Angeles Times article ("Tokyo Awaits Arrival of Downey Hose") quoted a message from Tokyo stating, "Tell Di Peso in Downey the other end of his hose has not turned up here, but we're all still looking." The hose eventually vanished entirely, and the most likely explanation was an underground river pulling it down. In the early 1960s, a rumor circulated that Downey's City Library had banned Edgar Rice Burroughs' Tarzan books because Tarzan was not married to Jane when they conceived Boy. This rumor was perpetuated in Los Angeles Times articles from the 1970s, such as "Downey Sends L.A. Back to the Bush League" (May 8, 1970). However, the rumor was false; according to "Zane Grey Also Safe: Tarzan’s Marital Status No Issue as Downey School Ban Is Denied" (December 28, 1961), a parent had placed two Zane Grey books "out of site in a desk drawer" in one elementary school, and no Tarzan books were removed. The books were later returned to the shelves. Most of Downey lies within the Downey Unified School District, with its two main public high schools named after Governor John G. Downey and Governor and Chief Justice Earl Warren. Downey has three public high schools: Downey, Warren, and Columbus High School. Other public schools are located in the Montebello Unified School District, Little Lake City Elementary School District, and Whittier Union High School District. Private schools are available, and Roman Catholic schools fall under the Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Los Angeles. The Downey City Library serves the city; the first library was established in 1901 by a women's social club founded in 1898. The County of Los Angeles Public Library opened a branch in Downey in September 1915, which moved several times, ending at the County Civic Center. In 1958, the Downey City Council voted to establish its own library and leave the county system. City library services initially operated from the back of a bookstore and opened on July 1, 1958, in the former cafeteria of the Downey Elementary School, which was then used as city hall and police station. A permanent building was constructed on December 7, 1959, with nearly 16,000 square feet (1,500 m²) and a cost of $186,200, or $11.97 per square foot, and was dedicated on December 17 and opened on December 18. In February 1984, an addition of nearly 12,000 square feet (1,100 m²) was completed and dedicated. In March 2019, the city announced it would use Measure S funds to begin remodeling the library, originally scheduled for 15 months but delayed by the COVID-19 pandemic. The remodeled library opened on May 3, 2021, with features including mobile app support for checkouts and a multi-use community space. The headquarters of the County of Los Angeles Public Library are located in Downey. The Los Angeles County Department of Public Health operates the Whittier Health Center in Whittier, which serves Downey. The United States Postal Service operates three post offices in Downey: the Downey Post Office at 8111 Firestone Boulevard, the North Downey Post Office at 10409 Lakewood Boulevard, and the South Downey Post Office at 7911 Imperial Highway. Los Cerritos Community News serves the city. Four freeways provide access to Downey: I-105 and the Metro C Line pass through the southern part, I-5 through the northern region, I-605 along the eastern side, and I-710 just west of the city. The Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority (Metro) provides bus services, with service available at the Lakewood Boulevard station on the C Line, and Downey also operates a local bus service called DowneyLINK. The Downey Patriot is a weekly community newspaper, while the Los Angeles Times and the Press-Telegram provide daily local coverage in Los Angeles County and the Gateway Cities region.
